The caption on Pelicot’s picture reads: ‘For years, I was ... by my husband.’ Composite: Alice Moitiê/Havas Paris Gisèle Pelicot Gisèle Pelicot’s daughter launches awareness campaign for potential victims of drugging and sexual assault Campaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attack Kim Willsher in Paris Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Gisèle Pelicot is the figurehead of a new campaign run by her daughter to encourage people who suspect they have been drugged and sexually assaulted to come forward, even if they have little to no memory of the attack. Caroline Darian, 47, who believes she was also drugged and assaulted by her father, Dominique Pelicot – her mother’s ex-husband – launched a primetime public information push on Monday across France’s television network, on social media, in the press and on posters. Her 73-year-old mother became an international symbol of courage and resistance when she insisted shame must change sides during the trial of her former husband and dozens of men who raped her while she was unconscious. Video clips featuring Gisèle Pelicot state that in 75% of cases of sexual abuse while drugged, the perpetrator is a relative or friend. She urges those who believe they may be victims to contact the Centre of Excellence on Substance-Facilitated Assaults (CRAFS). View image in fullscreen Another poster in the campaign reads: ‘On my birthday, I was … by my stepfather.’ Photograph: Alice Moitiê/Havas Paris The centre is attached to the Paris university hospital service (AP-HP) and staffed by experts who can suggest to those who believe they may have been a victim of drugging and abuse what evidence there might be and how it can be obtained. Caroline Darian, daughter of Gisèle Pelicot, speaks: ‘How can you rebuild when your father is the worst sexual predator in decades?’ Read more Darian, the founder of the association Mendorspas (Don’t Put Me to Sleep), said: “When you launch a campaign of this scale, having my mother’s backing sends a really powerful message. It’s also a message of hope for victims, showing that it is possible to get back on your feet.” The trial of Dominique Pelicot two years ago shocked the world. For almost a decade he had drugged his wife, raped her and invited strangers into their home in the village of Mazan, 20 miles from Avignon, to rape her while she was in a state of near coma. Pelicot’s horrific ordeal might have gone unremarked had she not decided to waive her anonymity and insist the case be held in public. Dominique Pelicot and 50 other men were convicted. The trial sparked the reporting of other cases of what UK police call drug-facilitated sexual abuse, or DFSA. Earlier this month, a man in his 60s pleaded guilty to drugging and raping his wife over two decades and inviting strangers to abuse her, in the latest in a string of similar crimes. After the publication of her book A Hymn to Life: Shame Has to Change Sides earlier this year, Pelicot said: “Shame sticks to you, it sticks to your skin. And that shame is a double sentence, it’s a suffering you inflict on yourself.” View image in fullscreen This poster’s caption reads: ‘Last night, I was … by my brother.’ Photograph: Alice Moitiê/Havas Paris Darian told Le Parisien : “It’s not because someone doesn’t remember that there aren’t traces or tests possible. Our aim is that these women can take back their own stories, so they no longer feel ashamed or afraid of not being heard by the police, not believed by the legal system and not supported by their family or those close to them.” She added: “Launching a campaign on this scale is quite unprecedented for an issue that was not recognised at all as a public health concern as recently as five years ago. When I started campaigning, nobody had heard of it [chemical submission] apart from a small circle of doctors. The Mazan trial was a major turning point with a global reach. “We’re getting somewhere but the fight is far from over. The message we want to send is that if you have a doubt, you need to look into it. Just because you cannot remember something, doesn’t mean there are no traces of it.” Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). The union described VW's vision for the future of work at the Wolfsburg-based giant as a "catalog of horrors." VW, the world's second-largest car company by both sales and production, has seen profits nosedive — it announced quarterly losses of €5.8 billion ($6.5 billion) in October — for a number of reasons, ranging from increased competition to tariffs and soft sales. Now the company plans to slash 120,000 jobs at 10 brands by 2030. Arguing that its financial outlook has "deteriorated," VW management says it has no choice but to make deeper cuts faster than expected. VW wants to scrap the current contract's 35-hour week and is demanding employees work overtime without pay if needed and went so far as to announce that pay would be "adjusted" if workers were forced to work fewer than 35 hours. Moreover, it is calling for a pay freeze for 2027-2028, as well as cuts to benefits for long-term employees. IG Metall says workers haven't seen a raise since May 2024 and is calling for a 5% hike now, citing ever-rising living costs. Regional IG representative Thorsten Gröger said, "VW management is stabbing its employees the back." He added that negotiations will be "tenacious, bitter and exhausting" and that they "will leave deep scars at the company." Workers are primed for walkouts , with the union warning that the battle may be far larger than anything VW has ever seen. VW works council chairwoman Daniela Cavallo, who represents employees within the company, said, "Management's promises are obviously worthless." Cavallo said workers felt "betrayed" after they agreed to major job cuts for the health of the company two years ago. The current contract applies to some 130,000 employees at German production sites in Braunschweig, Chemnitz, Dresden, Emden, Hanover, Kassel, Salzgitter, Wolfsburg and Zwickau. Speaking during a visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau , a former concentration camp , Pistorius said the site bore witness to the worst of Nazi Germany's crimes, calling it an absolute low point. "It all started with defining what made a life unworthy; by dividing according to race, origin, faith, sexual orientation," Pistorius warned, saying that such marginalization was experiencing a "renaissance" and "gaining ground with far-right extremist parties across Europe." The defense minister said Auschwitz provides all people, but particularly Germans, with a "symbol warning that we all bear responsibility for what happens and what must not be allowed to happen." During his tour of the camp, Pistorius laid a wreath at its death wall, where Nazi soldiers shot roughly 5,000 prisoners dead, and lit a candle at the victims' memorial . Edited by: Sean Sinico https://p.dw.com/p/5PexL Skip next section AfD politician accuses Le Pen of abandoning party 'core' 11/19/2026 November 19, 2026 AfD politician accuses Le Pen of abandoning party 'core' Mark Hallam Sven Tritschler is seen as an ally of Alice Weidel and an advocate of the party avoiding any moves towards relative moderation akin to those touted by right-wing leaders in France or Italy Image: Revierfoto/dpa/picture alliance The deputy chairman of Germany's right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) has accused French presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen of deserting her core values in her bid to achieve wider popularity and improve her chance of victory in French presidential elections . For years, Le Pen claimed to be embarking on a policy of what's often called "de-demonization," trying to shed the extreme-right image of her father and predecessor, Jean-Marie Le Pen, and soften the stance of the party now called the National Rally or RN. "Mrs. Le Pen, whom we all once admired greatly, now seems to have one fundamental principle: I say whatever the polls demand of me," Sven Tristschler told the right-leaning website The Pioneer. France is headed into the last months of a presidential election campaign, with incumbent Emmanuel Macron's second and final term coming to an end and no clear candidate emerging as a main challenger to Le Pen as yet. "At the end of the day, her victory would likely be even more catastrophic for the right than her defeat," Tritscher asserted. "The citizens would think they were voting to the right, only to get another Macron in the end." He said that in hindsight, he was glad the AfD and RN parties had fallen out in European politics in recent years, and said AfD supporters should not anticipate a similar move toward moderation. "A hollowing-out will not take place with us," he said, using the German scientific term for enucleation, the removal of the internal nucleus or core of a cell. The AfD has made similar complaints about Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, accusing her party of a process of "Melonization" involving a softening of its core policy stances in a bid to retain power. A similar power struggle is thought to be brewing within the AfD itself as it remains far adrift of majority support despite regularly polling as the largest single party in Germany at present. Inflation had fallen to 2.9% from 3.3% in September after the German government introduced the fuel discount. But the central bank said the expiration of that fuel tax cut, along with other government measures, would drive inflation higher. The report also highlighted that natural gas prices are expected to rise. "On top of this, higher energy and input costs are expected to gradually feed through into the prices of other goods and certain services," the Bundesbank said. The merging of ​UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion ($1.4 trillion) in assets across two of the eurozone's largest economies. It would be one of the most significant cross-border ​European banking deals in years. In a statement to Reuters news agency, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said Germany "supports a swift process and an orderly transition of control." "We have reached common ground and UniCredit has ‌made clear commitments to Germany as a business location, to the rights of Commerzbank employees and to a continued constructive dialogue with ‌the works ​council," Klingbeil said, referring to a body of elected employee representatives. Among the concessions, Germany is said to have given up its insistence on naming two supervisory board members to Commerzbank. Meanwhile, UniCredit agreed to the key German demand to keep UniCredit's enlarged German business headquartered and listed in Frankfurt. UniCredit also reportedly pledged to put German nationals on UniCredit's board of directors.
